summary.headline: Stand up three guardrails before any support AI goes live: escalation/handoff rules, a read-only-first posture, and the retrieval plumbing.
summary.narrative: These are the non-negotiable guardrails for a Customer Success AI. Build them in order: wire the retrieval plumbing so grounding is reliable, deploy read-only-first so a wrong answer can't become a wrong action, and define explicit escalation triggers with a context-handoff template so humans pick up cleanly. None of this provisions an AI — it is the safety design a human implements.

findings.title: Define explicit escalation and handoff triggers
findings.what_we_found: By default a support AI has no rule for when to stop and hand to a human, so it will attempt answers it shouldn't.
findings.why_it_blocks_ai: Without hard handoff triggers, the AI self-serves sensitive or low-confidence cases and gives wrong or unsafe answers.
the_fix: Hand off on any of: low retrieval confidence, a sensitive intent (billing / account security / legal-regulated), two failed turns on the same question, explicit customer request, or detected frustration.
Route each sensitive class to its named human queue.
Attach the context-handoff template (see draft) to every escalation so the human has full context.
findings.evidence: Generated best-practice guardrail; no AI deployment should ship without it.

findings.title: Deploy read-only-first — humans commit every write
findings.what_we_found: A first-deployment AI is often given write access (record updates, status changes, refunds) before its accuracy is proven.
findings.why_it_blocks_ai: Write access on day one turns a single wrong answer into a wrong action — an erroneous refund, a changed record, a closed case.
the_fix: Grant the AI integration user read and draft permissions only; no create/update/delete on customer records.
Require a human to commit any write the AI proposes.
Stage write access only after a monitored read-only period passes review.
findings.evidence: Generated best-practice guardrail (least privilege, staged enablement).

findings.title: Wire and verify the retrieval plumbing before grounding
findings.what_we_found: Knowledge retrieval depends on Data Category Visibility, FLS on Knowledge fields, and sharing — commonly misconfigured so the AI either retrieves nothing or sees internal-only content.
findings.why_it_blocks_ai: Wrong visibility starves retrieval (no grounding) or leaks internal articles into customer answers.
the_fix: Set Data Category Visibility so the AI integration user sees exactly the public KB categories.
Confirm field-level security on every Knowledge field the AI reads (title, body, summary).
Set sharing rules to expose only published, customer-facing articles; exclude internal-only.
Run a least-privilege review: confirm the integration user sees the public KB and nothing internal.
findings.evidence: Generated best-practice checklist for Knowledge-grounded retrieval.
